Identifying a man by his mother rather than his father was unusual; whether the townspeople mean it as a slight is debated."},{"verse":11,"phrase":"as a testimony against them","lemma":"μαρτύριον","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"for a testimony against them","note":"The Greek says only 'as a testimony to them'. Shaking a place's dust from one's feet was a gesture of breaking off all association with it."},{"verse":12,"phrase":"turn back","lemma":"μετανοέω","kind":"departure","traditional":"repent","note":"The traditional 'repent' now suggests mainly feeling sorry. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term that readers understand to include a changed life."},{"verse":14,"phrase":"King Herod","lemma":"βασιλεύς","kind":"background","traditional":"King Herod","note":"This is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome with the lesser title of tetrarch. He was never formally a king. Mark's 'king' probably reflects popular local usage, though some read it as ironic."},{"verse":14,"phrase":"John the Baptizer","lemma":"βαπτίζω","kind":"departure","traditional":"John the Baptist","note":"Here and in verse 24 Mark uses a participle, 'the one who baptizes', and in verse 25 the noun that became the fixed title 'the Baptist'. The translation keeps the difference. Most English versions print 'the Baptist' throughout."},{"verse":20,"phrase":"a just and holy man","lemma":"δίκαιος","kind":"departure","traditional":"a righteous and holy man","note":"English divides one Greek word-family between 'just' and 'righteous'; this translation uses 'just' and 'justice' throughout so the family stays visible. Most translations use 'righteous', which better suggests right standing before God but hides the link to ordinary justice. Both words lose something."},{"verse":20,"phrase":"he was greatly perplexed","lemma":"ἀπορέω","kind":"textual","traditional":"he did many things","note":"Many later manuscripts read a similar-looking verb, giving 'he did many things', which is the reading behind the King James Version. The earliest witnesses read 'he was greatly perplexed', which most modern editions and translations follow."},{"verse":22,"phrase":"Herodias’s own daughter","lemma":"","kind":"textual","traditional":"the daughter of Herodias herself","note":"The manuscripts are divided here. Some early and important ones read 'his daughter Herodias', which makes the girl Herod's daughter and gives her the same name as her mother; some critical editions print that reading. The text translated here makes her the daughter of Herodias, which agrees with Matthew's account. The Jewish historian Josephus names Herodias's daughter by her earlier marriage as Salome; Mark does not name her."},{"verse":23,"phrase":"up to half my kingdom","lemma":"βασιλεία","kind":"background","traditional":"unto the half of my kingdom","note":"The phrase echoes the Persian king's offer to Esther in the book of Esther and was a byword for extravagant generosity. As a ruler who held his territory at Rome's pleasure, Antipas had no kingdom he could actually give away."},{"verse":37,"phrase":"two hundred denarii","lemma":"δηνάριον","kind":"background","traditional":"two hundred pennyworth","note":"A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day's pay for a laborer. Two hundred denarii is therefore more than half a year's wages."},{"verse":40,"phrase":"plot by plot","lemma":"πρασιά","kind":"departure","traditional":"in groups / in ranks","note":"The Greek word means a garden bed, and Mark doubles it ('plots plots'), just as he doubles the word for a dining party in verse 39. The picture is of orderly rectangles of people laid out on the grass like beds in a garden. Most translations flatten both expressions to 'in groups'."},{"verse":48,"phrase":"the fourth watch of the night","lemma":"φυλακή","kind":"background","traditional":"the fourth watch of the night","note":"By Roman reckoning the night was divided into four watches. The fourth was the last, roughly three to six in the morning, so the disciples had been rowing most of the night."},{"verse":48,"phrase":"He meant to pass by them","lemma":"παρέρχομαι","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"he would have passed by them","note":"The Greek says plainly that he wanted or intended to pass by them, which puzzles many readers. A widely held view is that 'pass by' echoes the language of Israel's Scriptures for God passing by to reveal himself, as to Moses and Elijah, so that the intent is to show himself and not to avoid them. Others take it as how things looked to the disciples: 'he seemed about to pass them'."},{"verse":50,"phrase":"it is I","lemma":"ἐγώ εἰμι","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"it is I","note":"The Greek is literally 'I am'. It is the ordinary way to say 'It's me', and that is its surface meaning here. It is also the phrase the Greek Scriptures use for God's self-declaration, and in a scene of walking on the sea many interpreters hear that overtone as well; how much Mark intends it is disputed."},{"verse":56,"phrase":"the fringe of his cloak","lemma":"κράσπεδον","kind":"background","traditional":"the border of his garment / the hem of his garment","note":"The word can mean simply the edge of a garment. It is also the term the Greek Scriptures use for the tassels that the Law told Israelite men to wear on the corners of their cloaks. Either may be meant here; 'fringe' leaves both possible."}]}

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He left there and came to his hometown, and his disciples followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the Sabbath came, he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astounded, saying,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “Where did this man get these things? What is this wisdom that has been given to him, and what are these deeds of power done through his hands?

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And aren’t his sisters here with us?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they took offense at him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own household.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he could not do any deed of power there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he was amazed at their unbelief. Then he went around the surrounding villages, teaching.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He called the twelve to him and began to send them out two by two, and he gave them authority over the unclean spirits.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He instructed them to take nothing for the road except a staff alone: no bread, no bag, no money in their belts,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but to wear sandals, and not to put on two tunics.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Wherever you enter a house, stay there until you leave that place.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And whatever place does not welcome you, and they refuse to listen to you, as you leave there shake off the dust that is under your feet as a testimony against them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they went out and proclaimed that people should turn back,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they drove out many demons, and anointed many sick people with oil and healed them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: King Herod heard of it, for Jesus’s name had become well known, and people were saying,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “John the Baptizer has been raised from the dead, and that is why the powers are at work in him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But others were saying,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “He is Elijah,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and others were saying,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “A prophet, like one of the prophets.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when Herod heard of it, he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “John, the man I beheaded, has been raised!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Herod himself had sent men and arrested John and bound him in prison on account of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, because he had married her.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For John had been telling Herod,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Herodias held a grudge against him and wanted to kill him, but she could not,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for Herod feared John, knowing him to be a just and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he listened to him he was greatly perplexed, and yet he liked to listen to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then an opportune day came, when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles, his military commanders, and the leading men of Galilee.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Herodias’s own daughter came in and danced, and she pleased Herod and his dinner guests. The king said to the girl,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Ask me for whatever you want, and I will give it to you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he swore to her,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Whatever you ask me I will give you, up to half my kingdom.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She went out and said to her mother,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What should I ask for?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The head of John the Baptizer.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once she hurried back in to the king and made her request:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I want you to give me, right now, on a platter, the head of John the Baptist.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The king was deeply distressed, yet because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to refuse her.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So at once the king sent an executioner and ordered him to bring John’s head. He went and beheaded him in the prison,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: brought his head on a platter, and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his corpse and laid it in a tomb.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The apostles gathered around Jesus and reported to him all that they had done and all that they had taught.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Come away by yourselves to a deserted place and rest a while.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For many were coming and going, and they had no chance even to eat.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they went away in the boat to a deserted place by themselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there together on foot from all the towns and arrived ahead of them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he came ashore he saw a large crowd, and he felt compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd; and he began to teach them many things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the hour was already late, his disciples came to him and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This is a deserted place, and the hour is already late.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Send them away, so that they can go to the surrounding farms and villages and buy themselves something to eat.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You give them something to eat.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are we to go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “How many loaves do you have? Go and see.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had found out, they said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Five, and two fish.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he ordered them to have everyone recline, party by party, on the green grass.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they lay down, plot by plot, in hundreds and in fifties.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, said the blessing, and broke the loaves, and he kept giving them to his disciples to set before the people; and he divided the two fish among them all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They all ate and were satisfied,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they picked up broken pieces, twelve basketfuls, and some of the fish as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who had eaten the loaves were five thousand men.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once he made his disciples get into the boat and go on ahead to the other side, toward Bethsaida, while he himself dismissed the crowd.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After taking leave of them, he went off to the mountain to pray.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When evening came, the boat was in the middle of the sea, and he was alone on the land.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He saw them hard pressed at the oars, for the wind was against them, and about the fourth watch of the night he came toward them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but when they saw him walking on the sea, they thought it was a ghost and cried out,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for they all saw him and were terrified. But at once he spoke with them and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take courage; it is I. Do not be afraid.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he climbed into the boat with them, and the wind died down. And they were utterly astonished within themselves,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for they had not understood about the loaves; rather, their hearts had been hardened.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they got out of the boat, people at once recognized him

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and ran about that whole region and began to carry those who were ill around on their mats to wherever they heard he was.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And wherever he went, into villages or towns or farms, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and begged him to let them touch even the fringe of his cloak; and all who touched it were made well.

notes.note: The Greek word names a craftsman who builds, most often in wood but sometimes in stone. The traditional 'carpenter' is kept, though 'builder' or 'woodworker' would be equally defensible. Identifying a man by his mother rather than his father was unusual; whether the townspeople mean it as a slight is debated.

The Greek says only 'as a testimony to them'. This can mean evidence against them or a warning addressed to them, and most translations choose 'against'. Shaking a place's dust from one's feet was a gesture of breaking off all association with it.

The traditional 'repent' now suggests mainly feeling sorry. In the Gospels the word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term that readers understand to include a changed life.

This is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome with the lesser title of tetrarch. He was never formally a king. Mark's 'king' probably reflects popular local usage, though some read it as ironic.

Here and in verse 24 Mark uses a participle, 'the one who baptizes', and in verse 25 the noun that became the fixed title 'the Baptist'. The translation keeps the difference. Most English versions print 'the Baptist' throughout.

English divides one Greek word-family between 'just' and 'righteous'; this translation uses 'just' and 'justice' throughout so the family stays visible. Most translations use 'righteous', which better suggests right standing before God but hides the link to ordinary justice. Both words lose something.

Many later manuscripts read a similar-looking verb, giving 'he did many things', which is the reading behind the King James Version. The earliest witnesses read 'he was greatly perplexed', which most modern editions and translations follow.

The manuscripts are divided here. Some early and important ones read 'his daughter Herodias', which makes the girl Herod's daughter and gives her the same name as her mother; some critical editions print that reading. The text translated here makes her the daughter of Herodias, which agrees with Matthew's account. The Jewish historian Josephus names Herodias's daughter by her earlier marriage as Salome; Mark does not name her.

notes.traditional: unto the half of my kingdom
notes.note: The phrase echoes the Persian king's offer to Esther in the book of Esther and was a byword for extravagant generosity. As a ruler who held his territory at Rome's pleasure, Antipas had no kingdom he could actually give away.
A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day's pay for a laborer. Two hundred denarii is therefore more than half a year's wages.

The Greek word means a garden bed, and Mark doubles it ('plots plots'), just as he doubles the word for a dining party in verse 39. The picture is of orderly rectangles of people laid out on the grass like beds in a garden. Most translations flatten both expressions to 'in groups'.

notes.phrase: the fourth watch of the night
notes.traditional: the fourth watch of the night
notes.note: By Roman reckoning the night was divided into four watches. The fourth was the last, roughly three to six in the morning, so the disciples had been rowing most of the night.

notes.phrase: He meant to pass by them
notes.traditional: he would have passed by them
notes.note: The Greek says plainly that he wanted or intended to pass by them, which puzzles many readers. A widely held view is that 'pass by' echoes the language of Israel's Scriptures for God passing by to reveal himself, as to Moses and Elijah, so that the intent is to show himself and not to avoid them. Others take it as how things looked to the disciples: 'he seemed about to pass them'.

The Greek is literally 'I am'. It is the ordinary way to say 'It's me', and that is its surface meaning here. It is also the phrase the Greek Scriptures use for God's self-declaration, and in a scene of walking on the sea many interpreters hear that overtone as well; how much Mark intends it is disputed.

notes.traditional: the border of his garment / the hem of his garment
notes.note: The word can mean simply the edge of a garment. It is also the term the Greek Scriptures use for the tassels that the Law told Israelite men to wear on the corners of their cloaks. Either may be meant here; 'fringe' leaves both possible.
